text: What do I think about racism? You guys like to ask me this question, probably because I've been an immigrant myself since 2010 and have lived in a lot of different places. As you may know, I am from Kazakhstan, but I lived in the US until 2019, and for the past five years I've lived in Germany. So I want to talk about how I think about racism and tell you a story about a situation that kind of changed my perspective on it. I should start by saying that overall, in my experience, most places I've lived have been quite tolerant, and I haven't faced that much, at least direct racism towards me. But here's the interesting thing. While a lot of people get racially profiled in one direction, when I came to the US in 2010, I kind of received three types of questions slash remarks slash jokes. They were the Borat questions, once again, I'm actually from Kazakhstan. There were the Asian remarks, because I'm Central Asian, and there were the Russian jokes, since I speak Russian. In the beginning, it was quite annoying, and I probably did take some of it relatively close to my heart. But it's hard to say if I ever received a direct hostile racist remark. Maybe that's partly because I did quite a bit of martial arts growing up, and people could sense I could push back, or maybe I was just lucky. There's another reason too, though. I don't think I saw racism the same way some other immigrants did. You'd hear stories from other international people, they'd say, oh, they're racist, they did this or said that. And sometimes I'd find myself questioning it. Is that really racism? Am I too thick-skinned and others a bit too soft? Or am I just not seeing racism for what it is? But the more I thought about how I'd actually define racism, the more I came to a conclusion. A lot of what people call racism isn't really racism, it's ignorance. And again, this is my personal opinion. Some people make jokes or ask questions not from a place of hostility, but from a place of ignorance. For example, many Americans know very little about Kazakhstan, so sometimes they might ask weird questions like, do you guys have shopping malls there? Or do you have skyscrapers? Stuff like that. And if it comes from a place of ignorance without an actual intent to offend me, I don't think that's racism. Now, if it comes from a place of hostility, if someone specifically uses my race, my skin color, or my background to insult me, now that's racism. And there was one situation that kind of solidified this opinion in me. I remember one day a group of us international students were sitting in a dining hall. We were talking about pets. Some were saying, oh, I have a dog, I have a cat, I have some other pets. And then suddenly, one of the girls, I believe she was from Kenya, but I don't remember exactly, was like, I have a lion. Everyone got shocked, me included. We're all like, seriously? Tell us more. And she was like, yeah, we Africans have pet lions. Sometimes when you are a kid, you are given a baby lion, so you grow up with them. And everyone was like, damn, this is so cool. And then after a pause, the girl was like, are you guys freaking kidding me? Do you think that because I'm African, I have a pet lion? That was a joke. And suddenly, everyone felt a bit uncomfortable, me included, because I didn't know much about Kenya or Africa in general. And in my mind, for a second, I thought it was true. But I realized this came from a place of ignorance, not hostility. And how was I any different from those Americans who asked me about Kazakhstan or Borat? They just didn't know much about me or my country. And they most probably didn't want to offend me. So to me, that's not racism. Because it seems like I'm no different from them when it comes to the topics I'm ignorant about. So that's my little story. Hope you liked it. And maybe it gave you a new perspective on how to perceive what is racism. My name is Ilyas Abdullin. Thank you. And bye.
